e.meaning: gift of God, by way of Teodoro or Mateo
e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of Theo, short for Teodoro (Theodore) and also for Mateo and Teofilo. Teodoro comes from Greek theos, god, and doron, gift.
From the French surname Leroy, le roi, the king, a nickname for someone who acted like a king or served one. It became an American first name in the 1800s.
namesakes: Leroy Jethro Gibbs (lead character of NCIS)

assoc.t: Bad, Bad Leroy Brown, 1973 Jim Croce hit song
Leeroy Jenkins, a World of Warcraft video meme

e.note: Leeroy Jenkins, yelled in a famous 2005 World of Warcraft video, is a lasting internet meme that people still shout.

e.meaning: Zion, the hill of Jerusalem and the promised land
e.etymology: A respelling of Zion, from Hebrew Tsiyon, the hill in Jerusalem that came to stand for the city, the promised land and heaven. The root meaning of the Hebrew word is not known.
Either a blend of Emma and Lynn or a respelling of Emmeline, a medieval name the Normans brought to England, from a Germanic root meaning work.
A German surname from Adler, eagle, first given to someone who lived at a house marked with an eagle sign or who seemed eagle-like. Its use as a first name is recent and mostly American.
In Japan a girls' name: akari is the word for light or lamplight, and the name is written with several characters. In the US it is given more often to boys, alongside names like Dakari and Amari.

From Zen, the Japanese school of Buddhism, whose name comes through Chinese chan from Sanskrit dhyana, meditation. In English the word also means calm and composed, which is how it became a given name.

assoc.t: Zen Buddhism, the Japanese school of meditation
zen, meaning calm and at peace

e.meaning: the sturdy cotton cloth of blue jeans
e.etymology: The English word for the cotton twill used in jeans, from French serge de Nimes, cloth from the city of Nimes. It is a recent American given name, used for boys and girls.

assoc.t: denim, the fabric of blue jeans

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Ernest, from German Ernst, which comes from an old Germanic word meaning seriousness or resolve.
namesakes: Ernesto de la Cruz (singing villain of Pixar's Coco)

e.meaning: from Ainhoa, a Basque village with a shrine to the Virgin Mary
e.etymology: From the Virgin of Ainhoa, a title of Mary taken from a village in the French Basque Country. It is a popular girls' name across Spain.
A modern American name, a respelling of the surname Briley that also echoes Bryn, Riley and Kylie.
From Sanskrit vihana, dawn or morning. It is a popular modern boys' name in India and among Indian American families.
A modern Indian name, from Hindi Sanvi. It is widely explained as a name of the goddess Lakshmi, though it has no agreed Sanskrit root.
An American surname of uncertain origin, first given in honor of the writer Richard Henry Dana Jr. In Czech and other languages Dana is a separate name, a feminine form of Dan or short for Daniela.
namesakes: Dana Scully (FBI agent on The X-Files)

e.etymology: Used by George R. R. Martin for Lyanna Stark and Lyanna Mormont in A Song of Ice and Fire, and taken up by parents after the Game of Thrones TV series. It can also be read as a spelling of Liana.

assoc.t: Lyanna Stark and Lyanna Mormont, Game of Thrones

e.etymology: A spelling of Eloise shaped by Louise. Eloise comes from Old French Heloise, a name of Germanic origin made famous by the medieval scholar Heloise, the beloved of Abelard.
A short form of Dashiell and an English surname, from de Ash, for someone who lived near an ash tree. It also reads as the word dash, a quick burst of speed.
namesakes: Dash Parr (the super-fast son in Pixar's The Incredibles)

assoc.t: dash, a quick sprint or the punctuation mark
Dash, the speedy son in The Incredibles

e.etymology: The English word blessing used as a name, in the tradition of virtue names such as Grace and Faith. It is especially common in Nigeria and other English-speaking African countries.

assoc.t: blessing, the everyday word for a gift or favor from God

e.etymology: The short form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add, and now and then of Joel or Josiah. It has long been given as a full name in its own right.

assoc.t: a cup of joe, slang for coffee
sloppy joe, the saucy ground-beef sandwich
G.I. Joe, Hasbro's military action figures

e.meaning: valley of the wolf; a title of the Virgin Mary
e.etymology: From Our Lady of Guadalupe, the title of the Virgin Mary as patron of Mexico. The title comes from a place in Extremadura, Spain, whose name joins Arabic wadi, valley or river, with Latin lupus, wolf.

assoc.t: Our Lady of Guadalupe, patron saint of Mexico
Guadalupe River and Guadalupe Mountains in Texas

e.etymology: A one-t spelling of Matthew, from Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of Yahweh. Matthew was one of the twelve apostles and the traditional author of the first Gospel.

e.meaning: fiery, by association with Latin ignis, fire
e.etymology: The Spanish form of Ignatius, from the Roman family name Egnatius, later respelled to match Latin ignis, fire. It honors Saint Ignatius of Loyola, the Basque founder of the Jesuits.
e.note: The usual Spanish nickname is Nacho, which English speakers know as the snack.

e.etymology: From an Irish surname whose exact Gaelic source is uncertain. It rose in the US around 2010 with actor Kellan Lutz of the Twilight films.
namesakes: Kellan Lutz (actor in the Twilight films)

e.etymology: A modern feminine spelling of Aubrey, the Norman French form of the Germanic name Alberic, from words for elf and ruler. Aubrey was a men's name until the late 20th century.

e.meaning: sign, miracle; a verse of the Quran
e.etymology: From Arabic aya, a sign or wonder, the word used for each verse of the Quran. It is spelled Aya as often as Ayah.
The Persian form of Arabic Thurayya, the name of the Pleiades, the cluster of stars in Taurus. The word was also used for a brilliant gem or chandelier.
A respelling of Carson, a Scottish surname of uncertain origin that became an American first name. The -yn ending is most often chosen for girls.
An Italian short form of Giovanni, the Italian John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. In Italy it mostly begins compound names such as Gianluca and Giancarlo.
The Spanish form of Philip, also the usual form in Brazil, from Greek Philippos: philein, to love, and hippos, horse. It was the name of kings of Macedon and of Spain.
The French form of Angelica, from Latin angelicus, angelic, which goes back to Greek angelos, messenger. English speakers took it up in the 20th century.
A spelling of Devin, from an Irish surname linked to Gaelic words for poet and for fawn; Devin is also a form of the surname Devine. The y spelling is given mostly to girls.

e.meaning: lord, ruler; a name of the god Shiva
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Ishana, ruler or lord, a name of Shiva and of the Hindu guardian deity of the northeast.
